Question 74. Dimension of complementary projection components

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original hard proof problem

Let a linear map P:V→V satisfy P2=P, with V finite-dimensional. Prove V=imP⊕kerP without assuming orthogonality.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

For any v, write v=Pv+(v−Pv). The first part is in the image; the second is in the kernel because P(v−Pv)=Pv−P2v=0. Thus the two spaces span V. If w=Pu also lies in the kernel, then 0=Pw=P2u=Pu=w, proving trivial intersection. The decomposition is therefore unique, and the component dimensions sum to dimV. No inner product entered the proof. The projection may be oblique; idempotence alone does not imply a symmetric matrix or perpendicular components.

Question 75. Intersection dimension from ranks of stacked constraints

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original hard problem

Let U=kerA and W=kerB in Fn. Derive formulas for dimensions of the intersection and sum in terms of matrix ranks.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The intersection is the kernel of the vertical stack C=[AB], because a vector must satisfy both systems. Thus dim(U∩W)=n−rankC. Separately dimU=n−rankA and dimW=n−rankB. Substituting into the two-space dimension formula gives dim(U+W)=n−rankA−rankB+rankC. Dependencies between the two sets of constraint rows are measured by the stacked rank. For ranks two and three in n=6 with stacked rank four, the intersection dimension is two and the sum dimension is five.

Question 76. A quotient of polynomial spaces

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original hard problem

In P4(ℝ), let U be the polynomials divisible by x2−1. Construct a quotient basis and an explicit coordinate formula.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The subspace U has basis x2−1,x(x2−1),x2(x2−1) and dimension three. Polynomial division by the monic quadratic gives each polynomial a unique remainder a+bx. Therefore the cosets 1+U,x+U form a quotient basis, of dimension two. For p=c0+c1x+c2x2+c3x3+c4x4, reducing powers by x2=1 modulo U yields coordinates (c0+c2+c4,c1+c3). The remainder map is linear, its kernel is exactly U, and its surjectivity is clear from linear polynomials. The polynomial equality x2=1 holds only in the quotient, not in the original polynomial space.

Question 77. A hard counterexample to distributivity of subspaces

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original hard conceptual problem

Is U∩(W+Z)=(U∩W)+(U∩Z) always true? Establish the valid inclusion and provide a strict counterexample.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

A vector in the right side is a sum of two vectors both in U, one in W and the other in Z. It therefore belongs to U and W+Z, proving right-side inclusion in the left. For strictness in ℝ2, take U=span(e1+e2), W=spane1, and Z=spane2. Then W+Z=ℝ2, so the left side is the nonzero line U. Both individual intersections on the right are zero, so the right side is zero. Familiar set distributivity cannot simply be transplanted with subspace sum replacing union.

Question 78. A valid modular identity

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original hard proof problem

Assume U⊆Z. Prove U+(W∩Z)=(U+W)∩Z.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

If x=u+w with u∈U and w∈W∩Z, then both summands lie in Z because U⊆Z. Thus x∈(U+W)∩Z. Conversely let x∈(U+W)∩Z, so x=u+w for some u∈U,w∈W, and x∈Z. Since u∈Z, subtraction gives w=x−u∈Z. Hence w∈W∩Z and x∈U+(W∩Z). This proves equality. The containment premise is used in both directions and distinguishes this valid identity from the false unrestricted distributive identity.

Question 79. Extending a prescribed basis using another supplied basis

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original hard synthesis problem

Let U,W⊆V have dimensions three and three, with intersection dimension one. Can one always choose a basis of U+W consisting of all three members of a prescribed basis of U and two vectors from a prescribed basis of W? Prove your answer.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

Yes. The union of the prescribed basis lists spans U+W, whose dimension is 3+3−1=5. Begin with all three prescribed U vectors, an independent list. Process the three prescribed W vectors and retain a vector exactly when it is outside the current span. Each retained vector preserves independence. At termination the retained list spans the union and hence the sum. It is therefore a five-vector basis, so exactly two W vectors were retained. It is not necessarily possible to discard an arbitrarily chosen W vector; the decision depends on its position relative to the current span. The constructive extension argument proves existence without assuming compatible initial bases.

Question 80. Independent constraints on a direct sum

Original or independently reconstructed course problem · Foundational checks and Medium–Hard synthesis

Original hard capstone problem

Let V=U⊕W, with dimensions four and three. Let a nonzero functional ℓ:V→ℝ be nonzero on both U and W. Find dimkerℓ, dim(U∩kerℓ), dim(W∩kerℓ), and determine whether these last two spaces sum to the kernel.

Read the complete solution and reasoning

The ambient dimension is seven. A nonzero scalar functional has rank one, so its kernel has dimension six. Its restriction to U is nonzero and has rank one, so the restricted kernel has dimension three. The corresponding dimension on W is two. These two restricted kernels intersect trivially because U∩W=0, so their sum has dimension five. It is a proper subspace of the six-dimensional full kernel. The missing direction comes from cancellation across components: choose u∈U with ℓ(u)=1 and w∈W with ℓ(w)=−1. Then u+w∈kerℓ, although neither component lies in its restricted kernel. Thus a constraint on a direct sum need not split into separate zero constraints on each component.

27. Final examination rules, conditions, and worked checks

Rule 1

Closure through a homogeneous equation. A nonzero homogeneous scalar constraint on ℝn leaves dimension n−1. For x+2y−z=0, the basis (−2,1,0),(1,0,1) proves dimension two; checking the free coordinates proves independence.

Rule 2

An affine plane is not a subspace. A consistent system Ax=b≠0 is an affine translate of N(A), not a subspace. The plane x+2y−z=3 has affine dimension two but fails the zero-vector test.

Rule 3

Scaling closure does not give addition closure. Containing zero and being scaling-closed are insufficient for a subspace. The union of the two axes fails addition, whereas its span is ℝ2 of dimension two.

Rule 4

Modified operations with a shifted zero. For transported operations, identify the bijection before testing a basis. With c=(1,2) and φ(u)=u−c, the zero is c and a basis is (2,2),(1,3), whose translated vectors are e1,e2.

Rule 5

A false scalar multiplication axiom. When operations are changed, closure alone cannot replace all axioms. The rule a⋆(x,y)=(ax,0) fails 1v=v at (0,1); only its horizontal-axis restriction has the expected behavior.

Rule 6

Three parameters with only two freedoms. Count independent parameter directions, not parameter names. The map (a,b,c)↦(a+b,2a+2b,c) has a one-dimensional kernel and a two-dimensional image.

Rule 7

The logarithmic vector space. The zero vector need not be the number zero. In the positive-real space with multiplication as addition, zero is one, basis (2) gives [8](2)=3, and the additive inverse of eight is 1/8.

Rule 8

A homogeneous-looking nonlinear restriction. A zero right side does not make a nonlinear constraint a subspace condition. For p(0)p(1)=0, x and 1−x are admissible but their sum is not; the generated span still equals P2.

Rule 9

Dependent linear constraints. Subtract the rank of constraints rather than their raw count. In ℝ4, x1+x2+x3+x4=0, twice that same equation, and x1=x2 impose rank two, leaving dimension two.

Rule 10

A field restriction changes subspace status. Subspace status is relative to the scalar field. The real axis is a one-dimensional real subspace of ℂ, but is not a complex subspace because i·1 leaves it.

Rule 11

A dependency certificate from the original columns. Redundant generators create coefficient ambiguity. For (e1,e2,(2,3)), all representations of (5,7) have coefficients (5−2t,7−3t,t); the basis (e1,e2) restores uniqueness.

Rule 12

Joint independence versus pairwise tests. Pairwise independence does not imply joint independence. Three vectors in ℝ2 are always dependent; e1+e2−(e1+e2)=0 gives an explicit pairwise-nonparallel example.

Rule 13

Every vector need not be removable. A dependence permits solving only for a vector with a nonzero coefficient in the witness. In (e1,e2,2e2), the vertical entries are redundant individually, but removing e1 destroys the horizontal direction.

Rule 14

Independence of parameterized columns. Split parameter values before dividing by a potential pivot. The span of (1,t),(t,1) has dimension two off t=±1 and dimension one at both exceptional values.

Rule 15

A rank jump that a generic simplification hides. Test a new generator against the old span. With fixed vectors (1,0,1),(0,1,1), the column (a,b,1) is redundant exactly when a+b=1; the dimension is then two, otherwise three.

Rule 16

Transformed lists and a coefficient matrix. An invertible coefficient transformation preserves independence over the stated field. If u,v,w are independent, the list (u+v,v+w,w+u) has coefficient determinant two: it remains independent over ℝ, but has rank two in characteristic two.

Rule 17

A span equality with explicit recovery. Prove span equality by recovering both old generators. The replacement (u,v)↦(u+v,u−v) preserves span when two is invertible; over F2 it can collapse a plane to a line.

Rule 18

The exact relation space. The dependence space lives in coefficient space. Four generators of rank two have two independent relations; for v3=v1+v2,v4=2v1+v2, the relation basis is (−1,−1,1,0),(−2,−1,0,1).

Rule 19

Function independence from evaluation. Function independence concerns identities on the whole domain. Sampling 1,ex,e2x at 0,log2,log3 yields an invertible Vandermonde matrix of determinant two, proving independence.

Rule 20

A singular sample matrix is inconclusive. An invertible evaluation matrix proves independence; a singular one may only reflect poor nodes. The independent polynomials 1,x2 have identical samples at −1,1 but are separated by nodes zero and one.

Rule 21

Basis extraction from an echelon form. Use original pivot columns for column space, reduced nonzero rows for row space, and special solutions for nullspace. For A=[120324143625], the pivot columns are one and three, rank is two and nullity is two.

Rule 22

Why reduced columns may answer the wrong question. Row reduction preserves column dependency coefficients, not numerical column space. For A with columns (1,2),2(1,2), the reduced vector (1,0) is outside the original column space.

Rule 23

Extending a prescribed independent list. To extend an independent list, add a vector outside its span. The plane generated by (1,1,0),(0,1,1) satisfies y=x+z, so e1 supplies a valid third basis direction.

Rule 24

An allowed exchange and a forbidden exchange. A basis member can be replaced by w exactly when its coordinate in w is nonzero. For w=2e1−e2 over ℝ, replace e1 or e2, but not e3.

Rule 25

A dimension bound is not a spanning certificate. Exactly d vectors in dimension d form a basis only after independence or spanning is established. Four vectors (e1,e2,e3,e1+e2) in ℝ4 fail both requirements despite the correct count.

Rule 26

A maximal list relative to a candidate set. State the universe of maximality. A maximal independent sublist of e1,e2,e1+e2 is a basis of their plane, not of the larger space ℝ3.

Rule 27

Nonunique representation count over a finite field. Over Fq, a consistent system with nullity k has exactly qk solutions. A rank-three 4×7 matrix over F3 has 81 solutions per attainable right side and 27 attainable right sides.

Rule 28

A nested dimension chain. Proper finite-dimensional subspace inclusions force strict dimension inequalities. In a chain with endpoint dimensions five and seven and two proper inclusions, the middle dimension must be six.

Rule 29

Equal dimensions without inclusion. Equal finite dimensions imply subspace equality only with an inclusion premise. The xy and xz planes each have dimension two but are distinct; an inclusion between them would force equality.

Rule 30

Coordinates in a nonstandard basis. Always verify coordinates by reconstructing the original vector. The vector (3,1) has coordinates (2,1) in ((1,1),(1,−1)) and (1,1) in ((2,0),(1,1)).

Rule 31

Change-of-basis direction. The columns of PC←B are the C coordinates of the B vectors. For B=((1,1),(1,−1)) and C=((2,0),(1,1)), P=[011−1] sends (2,1)T to (1,1)T; reversing the conversion requires P−1.

Rule 32

Coordinates in a proper subspace. A basis of a proper subspace may give a rectangular basis matrix. The columns (1,0,1),(0,1,1) recover coordinates (2,3) for (2,3,5), but their 3×2 matrix has no ordinary two-sided inverse.

Rule 33

Dual coordinates as rows of the inverse. Rows of a square basis matrix inverse read its coordinates. For ((1,1),(1,−1)), the dual functionals are (x+y)/2 and (x−y)/2, giving coordinates (1,4) for (5,−3).

Rule 34

A polynomial basis with a triangular coefficient matrix. Coefficient comparison must use the selected basis. The polynomial 2+3x+4x2 has coordinates (−1,−1,4) in (1,1+x,1+x+x2), whose coefficient matrix has determinant one.

Rule 35

Distinct roots remove independent freedoms. In Pn, k distinct zero evaluations leave dimension n+1−k when k≤n+1. In P4 with roots zero, one, and two, a basis is r,xr for r=x(x−1)(x−2).

Rule 36

Repeated roots and derivative conditions. Over ℝ, p(1)=p'(1)=0 enforces a double root. Together with p(−1)=0 in P4, it gives basis r,xr with r=(x−1)2(x+1) and dimension two.

Rule 37

Dependent evaluation equations. Evaluation constraints must be ranked as functionals. In P3, p(0)=p(1)=0 already implies p(0)+2p(1)=0; the dimension is two rather than one.

Rule 38

A nonhomogeneous interpolation fiber. Nonzero interpolation data produce affine solution sets. The constraints p(0)=1,p(1)=2 in P3 give 1+x+(a+bx)x(x−1), with two free directions and no vector-subspace status.

Rule 39

Integral and derivative constraints. Linear functionals may involve integrals or derivatives. In P3, zero integral on [0,1] plus p'(0)=0 gives basis x2−1/3,x3−1/4 and dimension two.

Rule 40

All polynomials versus finite-support sequences. Algebraic span uses finite sums even for infinite generating sets. Monomials span all formal polynomials, while coordinate unit sequences span only finite-support sequences, excluding (1,1,1,…).

Rule 41

Symmetric matrices with zero trace. Symmetric trace-zero matrices have dimension n(n+1)/2−1 over ℝ. A basis uses off-diagonal symmetric pairs and Eii−Enn; the boundary n=1 has the empty basis.

Rule 42

Symmetric and skew-symmetric decomposition. The symmetric/skew decomposition requires two to be invertible. Over ℝ, the intersection is zero and dimensions sum to n2; in characteristic two the transpose equations coincide and the intersection is nonzero.

Rule 43

Two matrix constraints with a dependency. Zero row and column sums on real n×n matrices leave dimension (n−1)2. For n=3, four corner-adjusted Eij directions form a basis; the six sum constraints have one dependency.

Rule 44

Symmetry plus row sums. On symmetric matrices, zero row sums determine each diagonal independently. For order four, six off-diagonal freedoms remain, giving dimension six rather than nine or seven.

Rule 45

Commuting with a diagonal matrix. For diagonal D with distinct-value multiplicities mj, its commuting matrix space has dimension ∑jmj2. The multiplicities (2,1,1) give six allowed elementary-entry directions.

Rule 46

A nonlinear matrix set and its linear span. Singularity is not a linear constraint for matrix orders at least two. In order two, E11+E22=I disproves closure, while the singular elementary matrices span all of M2.

Rule 47

Polynomial parity and a direct sum. Real polynomials split uniquely into even and odd parts. In P5 each part has dimension three; 2+3x−4x2+x5 splits into 2−4x2 and 3x+x5.

Rule 48

A sum and intersection from explicit planes. Intersection directions measure ambiguity of decomposition. The xy and xz planes sum to ℝ3, share the x axis, and decompose (a,b,c) as (t,b,0)+(a−t,0,c).

Rule 49

Intersecting two equation-defined spaces. Solve simultaneous restrictions before applying the dimension formula. In ℝ4, let U satisfy x1+x2+x3+x4=0 and let W={(a,a,b,b)}. Dimensions are 3,2,1,4 for U,W,U∩W,U+W; characteristic two changes the intersection.

Rule 50

Intersection through generator coordinates. Equating basis expansions computes an intersection without guessing common generators. The patterns (a,b,a,b) and (c,c,d,d) meet on (t,t,t,t), so two planes have a three-dimensional sum.

Rule 51

Redundant generators inflate a block nullspace. The block-kernel dimension equals intersection dimension only when both generator matrices have independent columns. Duplicate e1 columns produce block nullity two for an intersection of dimension one.

Rule 52

Sharp intersection bounds. Intersection bounds need not determine a unique value. Two dimension-six subspaces in dimension ten can intersect in any dimension two through six; coordinate-subspace constructions prove sharpness.

Rule 53

Forced nonzero intersection. In finite dimension n, dimU+dimW>n forces a nonzero intersection. Replacing strictness by equality is invalid: two complementary coordinate planes in ℝ4 give equality and zero intersection.

Rule 54

Two-subspace union theorem. For exactly two subspaces, union closure is equivalent to containment. The witnesses u∈U∖W,w∈W∖U force u+w outside both; no real-field assumption is needed.

Rule 55

Three pairwise-trivial intersections are insufficient. For three spaces, pairwise zero intersections do not prove a direct sum. The three distinct lines generated by e1,e2,e1+e2 have total component dimension three but sum dimension two.

Rule 56

A nonorthogonal complement. A complement need not be orthogonal. The lines generated by (1,0) and (1,2) form a direct sum, with (5,6)=(2,0)+(3,6) despite a nonzero cross dot product.

Rule 57

The dimension formula does not extend by naïve inclusion-exclusion. Subspace dimensions do not obey naïve three-set inclusion-exclusion. Use the two-space formula iteratively; three distinct lines in a plane give predicted three by the naïve formula but actual dimension two.

Rule 58

Polynomial intersections and least common multiples. For divisibility subspaces, intersection uses the least common multiple. Factors x(x−1) and (x−1)(x−2) in P5 give dimensions four, four, three, and five for the two spaces, intersection, and sum.

Rule 59

A quotient basis from an adapted basis. Extend a subspace basis and take cosets of the added vectors. For U=span(1,1,0), the quotient basis e2+U,e3+U assigns coordinates (y−x,z) to (x,y,z)+U.

Rule 60

The quotient is not set subtraction. Cosets are equal exactly when their representatives differ by a subspace vector. Modulo the horizontal axis, (1,2) and (7,2) represent the same vector, and the quotient zero is the whole axis.

Rule 61

An annihilator with explicit equations. To compute an annihilator, impose zero values on a subspace basis. The plane generated by (1,1,0),(0,1,1) has annihilator spanned by x−y+z, of dimension one.

Rule 62

Restriction of scalars. Restricting complex scalars to reals doubles finite dimension. A complex basis v1,v2,v3 yields real basis v1,iv1,v2,iv2,v3,iv3, with six independent real directions.

Rule 63

Counting ordered bases. Ordered basis counting excludes the entire span of previous choices. In F23, the counts are 7,6,4, giving 168 ordered and 28 unordered bases.

Rule 64

Three proper finite-field subspaces can cover. The two-subspace union theorem must not be extended blindly to larger finite unions. Over F2, the three distinct lines in F22 cover all four ambient vectors.

Rule 65

Formal polynomial versus polynomial function. Over finite fields, formal polynomials and polynomial functions differ. On F3, x3−x is nonzero formally but vanishes everywhere, giving a one-dimensional kernel for evaluation on P3.

Rule 66

A proper subspace with equal infinite dimension. The inclusion-plus-equal-dimension equality test requires finite dimension. Both ℝ[x] and its proper subspace xℝ[x] have countably infinite monomial bases.

Rule 67

A parameterized intersection. Parameterized intersections may jump even when each component dimension stays fixed. For the planes z=0 and z=t(x+y), intersection dimension is two at t=0 and one otherwise.

Rule 68

Minimum constraints needed to specify a space. The minimal number of independent homogeneous scalar equations defining a subspace is its codimension. A four-dimensional subspace in ℝ7 requires exactly three, constructed from an adapted dual basis.

Rule 69

A finite-function space and constrained values. Functions on a finite set of size m form an m -dimensional coordinate space. One nonzero total-value constraint leaves dimension m−1; use point indicators minus one reference indicator as a basis.

Rule 70

Dimension of a recurrence solution space. Count independent initial data for a homogeneous recurrence. The second-order rule an+2=3an+1−2an has dimension two and basis sequences 1,2n, despite infinitely many coordinates.

Rule 71

Connected difference vectors. Connected edge differences span the sum-zero hyperplane. In ℝn its dimension is n−1, with basis ei−en; path telescoping explains why a spanning tree suffices.

Rule 72

A plane, a constrained intersection, and a normal direction. An equation-defined plane uses free-coordinate basis directions, while its coefficient row supplies a normal in Euclidean coordinates. For 2x−y+4z=0, use (1,2,0),(0,4,1) and normal (2,−1,4).

Rule 73

Measurement ambiguity and output dimension. Sensor ambiguity is a kernel, not a count of repeated outputs. The measurements x1+x2,x2+x3 have rank two and invisible direction (−1,1,−1), giving a one-parameter fiber for every output.

Rule 74

Dimension of complementary projection components. Every idempotent linear map splits its space into image and kernel. The decomposition v=Pv+(v−Pv) proves existence, and Pw=w on the image proves uniqueness; orthogonality is an additional property.

Rule 75

Intersection dimension from ranks of stacked constraints. For U=kerA,W=kerB⊆Fn, the stacked matrix C=[AB] defines their intersection. With ranks rA,rB,rC, dimensions are n−rC for the intersection and n−rA−rB+rC for the sum. Taking n=6,rA=2,rB=3,rC=4 gives two and five, respectively.

Rule 76

A quotient of polynomial spaces. Polynomial quotient coordinates can be read from remainders. Modulo multiples of x2−1 in P4, the basis cosets 1,x give coordinates (c0+c2+c4,c1+c3) and quotient dimension two.

Rule 77

A hard counterexample to distributivity of subspaces. Subspace sum and intersection are not generally distributive. The inclusion (U∩W)+(U∩Z)⊆U∩(W+Z) holds, but three distinct lines in a plane make it strict.

Rule 78

A valid modular identity. The modular identity requires U⊆Z. Under that premise, subtracting the U component keeps a vector in Z and proves U+(W∩Z)=(U+W)∩Z.

Rule 79

Extending a prescribed basis using another supplied basis. An independent subspace basis can be extended using a supplied spanning union. Two dimension-three spaces with one-dimensional intersection have a five-vector sum basis retaining any prescribed U basis and two suitably chosen W basis vectors.

Rule 80

Independent constraints on a direct sum. A scalar constraint can cancel across direct-sum components. For component dimensions four and three with nonzero restrictions, the full kernel has dimension six, while the sum of restricted kernels has only dimension five.

28. Editable exact-arithmetic laboratory

Enter generators as the columns of a small matrix and a target vector. The laboratory keeps the supplied generators unchanged, row-reduces a copy with exact rational arithmetic, identifies a basis from original pivot columns, constructs every nullspace basis direction, and decides target membership. Every row operation is shown. A dependent generator list has coefficient ambiguity, which must not be confused with ambiguity in the target vector itself.

Enter generators as columns: separate columns with commas and rows with semicolons. Use 2–4 rows, 1–5 columns and integer entries from −20 to 20. The target has one entry per row. Exact rational arithmetic handles every row operation, including fractions. The original generators are retained; an independently tracked row operator checks every intermediate matrix. Invalid input preserves the previous result. Every walkthrough starts paused.
